contributions.headingText:
The morphological correlates of hyperparathyroidism include parathyroid hyperplasia, parathyroid adenoma, and carcinoma. Accurate diagnosis of parathyroid disorders relies on clinical, laboratory, and genetic findings, along with detailed morphological assessment.

In this edition, for the first time, parathyroid hyperplasia is discussed. By definition, hyperplasia is a potentially reversible condition that is caused by a known stimulus. From such a perspective, secondary hyperplasia (most commonly attributable to chronic renal failure) represents the only true parathyroid hyperplasia. In tertiary hyperparathyroidism, autonomous hyperparathyroidism occurs as a result of hyperplasia-to-neoplasia progression. Despite evidence of neoplastic transformation, because tertiary hyperplasia is by definition always associated with pre-existing secondary hyperplasia and appears to represent a morphological and biological continuum, this is also discussed in the section on hyperplasia.

The individual parathyroid glands in the setting of advanced hyperplasia, particularly tertiary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic renal failure, may show highly atypical architectural features that can mimic carcinoma, including the presence of pseudoinvasion and a high proliferation index {32687943}. Although there is a risk of local recurrence or diffuse recurrence in the neck (parathyromatosis), distant metastasis is exceptional in the setting of renal failure–induced hyperparathyroidism {19836494; 32687943}. Therefore it is emphasized that the diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma should not be made in the setting of chronic renal failure in disease confined to the neck unless there is unequivocal vascular space invasion or very marked invasive growth – for example, unequivocal extension into adjacent organs such as the thyroid, oesophagus, or skeletal muscle {32687943}.

Despite the historical use of the term “hyperplasia” for the multiple endocrine neoplasia syndromes, hyperparathyroidism in these syndromes is almost always due to multiglandular/multinodular adenomas {11739416; 26163537; 32468209}. For this reason these are discussed in the section on parathyroid adenoma. In the context of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 it is again noted that although there is a high risk of local recurrence in the neck, distant metastasis is extremely rare, warranting similar strict criteria for malignancy to those applied in secondary/tertiary hyperplasia {32687943}.

An abnormal parathyroid gland is often enlarged and cellular, usually exceeding 8 mm and 60 mg {26163537}. The distinction between parathyroid adenoma and hyperplasia may not always be possible with certainty and a descriptive diagnosis such as “pathologically enlarged cellular (fat-depleted) parathyroid gland consistent with…” is often appropriate. The importance of proper macroscopic assessment and sampling of the specimen to ensure sectioning through the hilum of the gland is emphasized, because that is where the non-neoplastic tissue, used to support the diagnosis of adenoma over hyperplasia, is usually found.

The molecular genetics of parathyroid neoplasms (adenomas and carcinomas) have been elucidated, and although there is no need for routine immunohistochemistry in the majority of these tumours, there is a need to recognize the morphological features of inherited disease. Parafibromin-deficient tumours (those associated with CDC73 mutations) exhibit eosinophilic cytoplasm with perinuclear clearing, nuclear enlargement, microcystic change, and a sheet-like growth pattern {29324469}. The presence of multinodular multiglandular disease is a feature of inherited disease, and the role of molecular immunohistochemistry for parafibromin, menin, and p27 in facilitating the screening of CDC73-related, MEN1-related, and CDKN1B-related pathogenesis is discussed {29626276}.

Parathyroid lipoadenoma is discussed as an individual entity, unlike in previous editions, where it was included as a variant of parathyroid adenoma. The term “lipoadenoma” is only appropriate when there is an unequivocal increase in parenchymal parathyroid tissue as well as abundant adipose tissue, so parathyroid glands that are enlarged solely because of an increase in adipose tissue are not considered lipoadenomas {31773224}. The general rule that > 50% of the volume of the gland should be adipose tissue to warrant the diagnosis of lipoadenoma is recommended so that otherwise typical adenomas with only a small increase in fat are not considered lipoadenomas {26585863; 31773224; 32193823}.

The term “atypical parathyroid tumour”, defined as a parathyroid neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential that demonstrates atypical cytological and architectural features but lacks unequivocal features of malignancy, is introduced to replace previous terms such as “atypical parathyroid adenoma”. It is unclear how much cytological or architectural atypia is required to separate atypical parathyroid tumour from usual parathyroid adenoma. For instance, small areas of fibrosis, an occasional mitotic figure (< 5 mitoses/10 mm2), extension into but not through a thickened capsule, and a little contour irregularity not worrying for invasive growth are not uncommon in parathyroid adenomas and are insufficient to warrant designation as atypical parathyroid tumour, particularly if there has been previous manipulation or trauma of the gland {17021134; 28061891; 33740321}. Immunohistochemistry for various biomarkers associated with parathyroid carcinoma (e.g. parafibromin, PGP9.5, RB1, p53, galectin-3, E-cadherin, APC, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, MDM2, and BCL2) is often informative in the differential diagnosis. Although extremely rare, cases initially categorized as atypical parathyroid tumour with subsequent metastasis have been reported. However, current data on atypical parathyroid tumours suggest that they may be followed similarly to usual parathyroid adenomas in the absence of concerning clinical features or parafibromin deficiency {32687943; 31085770}. Therefore, although this diagnostic category should not be an excuse to avoid appropriate assessment, the only clinically relevant differential diagnosis for atypical parathyroid tumour is parathyroid carcinoma.

Reviews of the epidemiological data identified an increase in the worldwide incidence of parathyroid carcinoma {17372919; 22295377; 28362521; 29344163; 33738545}. The rigid pathological criteria for parathyroid carcinoma remain unchanged, requiring the presence of vascular invasion (angioinvasion), lymphatic invasion, perineural invasion, unequivocal invasion into adjacent structures or organs, or metastatic disease. The role of biomarkers in the diagnostic workup of parathyroid carcinoma is reviewed, along with the differential diagnosis. It is desirable to perform biomarker analysis routinely in parathyroid carcinomas. Among these biomarkers, parafibromin stands out as the most reliable biomarker of malignancy and also has the utility to inform germline screening for pathogenic CDC73 variants. Other somatic mutations identified in parathyroid carcinomas are discussed {33269427}. The prognostic role of angioinvasion characterized by tumour cells invading a vessel wall and intravascular tumour cells admixed with thrombus is emphasized {23001705; 31708875}. Like for other neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs), assessment of the proliferative activity of all parathyroid carcinomas by recording a formal Ki-67 proliferation index and mitotic count using standardized approaches is now recommended {32687943; 34079071}.
